tur44-0: Pain and morning stiffness in the Achilles tendon just above the heel: what is Achilles tendinopathy, how is it recognised, and which exercises help recovery? Recommendations of the 2024 guideline, a short history, six home exercises and warning signs.
tur44-1: Length of the loading exercise programmes found effective in studies
tur44-2: In a study of 58 patients, those satisfied with treatment at week 12 in the heavy slow resistance group; 80% with eccentric exercise (the difference was not significant)
tur44-3: In the same study, adherence to the heavy slow resistance programme; 78% for the eccentric programme
tur44-4: Sudden changes in training (distance, speed, hills), previous tendon problems or leg fractures, and fluoroquinolone antibiotics are among the risk factors; it becomes more common with age. According to the review reported in the US physiotherapy guideline, excess weight and foot posture were not associated with risk.
tur44-5: According to the American Physical Therapy Association's 2024 guideline, the diagnosis is mostly made from your history and an examination.
tur44-6: Pain brought on by load in the middle part of the tendon and tenderness when it is pressed are typical. Swelling in the tendon that moves along with the tendon when the ankle is moved (the arc sign), or a positive Royal London Hospital test, supports the diagnosis. Thickening of the tendon supports the diagnosis but may not always be present.
tur44-7: Usually not needed for the diagnosis. Ultrasound or MRI may be requested when the diagnosis is uncertain, recovery takes longer than expected, symptoms get worse or a procedure is being considered.
tur44-9: If the pain is a few centimetres above the heel, in the middle part of the tendon, it is midportion tendinopathy; if it is where the tendon attaches to the heel bone, it is insertional tendinopathy. In the latter, it is recommended that exercises be done without bending the ankle upwards (see Frequently asked questions).
tur44-10: Tendons get stronger by adapting to load that is increased gradually. The American Physical Therapy Association's 2018 guideline and its 2024 update also recommend loading exercises as the cornerstone of treatment; the update recommends doing the exercise at the highest tolerable load and at least 3 times a week, and staying active within pain limits rather than resting completely. The classic method is the eccentric programme developed by Alfredson and colleagues: slowly lowering the heel off a step twice a day for 12 weeks.
tur44-11: A study in Denmark of 58 patients compared this eccentric programme with heavy slow resistance exercise done three days a week. Both programmes clearly improved pain and function, and the gains were still present after 1 year. At week 12, satisfaction tended to be higher in the heavy slow resistance group (100% vs 80%; the difference was not statistically significant), while adherence to the programme was significantly higher (92% vs 78%).
tur44-13: Studies since the late 1990s have shown that the Achilles tendon heals with gradually increased load rather than with rest.
tur44-14: In a study of 15 recreational athletes, after 12 weeks of heavy-load eccentric calf exercise all patients had returned to their pre-injury running level; in the comparison group given conventional treatment, treatment was not successful and all patients ended up having surgery.
tur44-15: In a randomised study of 38 patients (AJSM), those who continued running and jumping while monitoring their pain and those who stopped these activities for the first 6 weeks improved similarly with the same exercise programme.
tur44-16: In a pilot study of 27 patients with pain where the tendon attaches to the heel, after a 12-week eccentric programme done without bending the ankle upwards, 67% of patients were satisfied and had returned to their previous activities at an average follow-up of 4 months.
tur44-17: In a study in the Netherlands using general practitioner records (BJSM), the yearly incidence of tendinopathy in the middle part of the Achilles tendon was 2.35 per 1,000 adults aged 21–60; a link with sport was recorded in 35% of cases.
tur44-18: In a study of 58 patients (AJSM), the eccentric programme and heavy slow resistance exercise were similarly effective; adherence was significantly higher in the heavy slow resistance group, and satisfaction at week 12 also tended to be higher.
tur44-19: The Achilles guideline of the American Physical Therapy Association (APTA) (JOSPT) was updated: loading exercises were recommended as the cornerstone of treatment.
tur44-20: The guideline's new update: loading exercise at the highest tolerable load as first-line treatment (A); together with education, and staying active rather than resting completely (B); low-level laser is no longer recommended (C); night splints continue not to be recommended (C).
tur44-21: A cortisone injection into the tendon is generally not recommended because of the risk of rupture; ask your physician whether it is suitable for you.
tur44-22: Treatment options: what does the guideline say?
tur44-23: Recommendations of the 2024 guideline (JOSPT) of the Academy of Orthopaedic Physical Therapy of the American Physical Therapy Association (APTA); the guideline covers tendinopathy in the middle part of the tendon. The letters in brackets are the recommendation grades (A strong, B moderate, C weak, D conflicting evidence, E theoretical evidence, F expert opinion). The guideline makes no recommendation on shockwave therapy because it considers it outside the scope of physiotherapy; treatment is chosen for each person.
tur44-25: Loading exercise at the highest tolerable load, first-line treatment (A); at least 3 times a week (E).
tur44-27: Education explaining the pain or the changes in the tendon, together with loading exercise, in person or remotely (B); it should be explained that complete rest is not needed and that activities can continue within pain limits (B).
tur44-29: Calf stretching if upward bending of the ankle is limited (C); manual therapy for movement restriction (F).
tur44-31: Elastic tape may be used to reduce pain or improve function, and rigid tape to reduce strain on the tendon or alter foot posture (E); evidence on orthoses is conflicting, no recommendation (D); a heel lift temporarily during activity (C).
tur44-33: Low-level laser should not be used (C); ultrasound therapy should not be used on its own (C); night splints should not be used (C).
tur44-34: May be considered for calf-related pain and stiffness, especially with recent-onset symptoms or when gradual loading is not tolerated (F).
tur44-35: Start with heel raises on both feet; as it gets easier, move on to one foot and to heel drops off a step. Do the movements slowly and with control. If your pain is where the tendon attaches to the heel, do not lower your heel below the level of the step during heel drops.
tur44-36: Put your hands on the wall and step your painful leg back. Keeping the back knee straight and the heel on the floor, move your hips towards the wall; feel a gentle stretch in your calf. It can be added to the programme if you have difficulty bending your ankle upwards; if your pain is where the tendon attaches to the heel, ask your physiotherapist or physician before doing this stretch.
tur44-37: Two basic techniques you can do on your own.
tur44-38: A cortisone injection into the Achilles tendon is generally not recommended, because it can weaken the tendon and increase the risk of rupture. Ask your physician whether it is a suitable option for you; regular loading exercises are usually tried first.
tur44-39: My pain is where the tendon attaches to the heel. Can I do the same exercises?
tur44-40: Largely yes, but with one difference. With pain where the tendon attaches to the heel (insertional tendinopathy), loading with the ankle bent upwards can press the tendon against the heel bone and increase the pain. In a pilot study of 27 patients, after a 12-week eccentric programme done without bending the ankle upwards, 67% of patients were satisfied and had returned to their previous activities at an average follow-up of 4 months. So during heel drops off a step, do not lower your heel below the level of the step; finish the movement on flat ground or level with the step.
tur44-41: In the following situations, seek help without delay.
tur44-42: A sudden "pop" or a feeling of being kicked in the heel, followed by being unable to rise onto your toes on that foot alone (the tendon may have ruptured)
tur44-43: Redness, warmth and swelling at the heel, especially together with a fever
tur44-44: Tendon pain or swelling that starts while taking a fluoroquinolone antibiotic or in the months after stopping it: rest the painful leg, pause the exercises and contact the physician who prescribed the medicine the same day; ask your physician whether to continue the medicine
tur44-45: Pain that does not improve within a few months despite regular exercise, or that keeps getting worse
tur44-46: European Medicines Agency. Disabling and potentially permanent side effects lead to suspension or restrictions of quinolone and fluoroquinolone antibiotics. 16 November 2018.
tur44-47: Lean your back against a wall with your feet one step in front of it. Keeping your knees in line with your toes, lower yourself to a depth that does not clearly increase the pain (knees bent at most halfway, as if sitting on a chair, not past 90 degrees), hold for a few seconds and come back up.
tur44-48: Cervical disc herniation and a pinched nerve causing arm pain: symptoms, which nerve goes where, what examination tests and MRI tell you, non-surgical treatment, a guideline comparison, a short history, home exercises and when surgery is needed.
tur44-49: Pinched nerves causing arm pain that newly appear each year in about 83 of every 100,000 people
tur44-50: According to a systematic review reported in the US physiotherapy guideline, the Spurling test picks up about half of pinched nerve roots (sensitivity 50%); a positive result supports the diagnosis (specificity 86–93%), while a negative result does not rule it out. Arm pain easing when the neck is gently lifted is a similar finding (sensitivity 44%, specificity 90–97%). Tests that tension the arm nerves, on the other hand, mainly help to rule out the diagnosis when they are negative. The guideline recommends relying not on a single test but on the history and examination findings assessed together. These tests are carried out by a physician or physiotherapist.
tur44-51: MRI shows where the herniation is, but it does not decide things on its own. Disc bulging was seen on MRI in 87.6% of 1,211 healthy volunteers with no neck or arm symptoms; even in people in their 20s the figure was 73–78%. What matters is whether the MRI finding matches the symptoms and the examination.
tur44-52: Understanding that arm pain can come from the neck
tur44-53: That arm pain can come from a disc in the neck was described in the 1940s. Later studies showed that most people recover without surgery and that MRI findings need to be interpreted together with symptoms.
tur44-54: The US neurosurgeon Roy Glenwood Spurling, together with Scoville, published a paper describing a sideways rupture of the neck discs as a common cause of shoulder and arm pain ("Lateral rupture of the cervical intervertebral discs"). Today Spurling's name is associated with an examination test used for arm pain.
tur44-55: In a population study in Rochester, Minnesota, of 561 patients diagnosed with a pinched nerve causing arm pain in 1976–1990 (Brain), the yearly incidence was about 83 per 100,000; at about 5 years of follow-up, 90% of patients, including those who had surgery, had no symptoms or only mild ones.
tur44-56: A systematic review of studies (Spine J): in arm pain caused by a cervical disc herniation, symptoms clearly improve within 4–6 months in most people.
tur44-57: Neck MRI scans of 1,211 healthy volunteers with no neck or arm symptoms were examined: 87.6% had disc bulging; even in people in their 20s the figure was 73–78%.
tur44-58: The neck pain guideline of the Orthopaedic Section of the American Physical Therapy Association (APTA) (JOSPT) was updated: for long-lasting (chronic) neck pain with arm pain, intermittent mechanical traction together with stretching and strengthening exercises and neck–upper back mobilisation or manipulation (B); education and advice encouraging participation in work and physical activity (B).
tur44-59: Symptoms are usually most intense in the first weeks. Most people clearly improve within 4–6 months; in a small study of 23 patients the improvement was maintained for 2–3 years, and complete recovery could take 2–3 years. In a population study in the USA that followed 561 patients diagnosed with a pinched nerve causing arm pain (from a herniation or osteoarthritis) in 1976–1990 for about 5 years, at the last check 90% of patients, including those who had surgery, had no symptoms or only mild ones; a quarter of the patients had had surgery during follow-up.
tur44-60: Avoiding movements that greatly increase the pain for a few days is often enough. The US physiotherapy guideline recommends education and advice that encourage participation in work and physical activity (B).
tur44-61: Exercises that strengthen the deep neck muscles and the area around the shoulder blades and stabilise the neck, together with nerve gliding exercises, may be part of treatment.
tur44-62: The US physiotherapy guideline (2017) recommends intermittent neck traction (controlled pulling of the neck) and mobilisation or manipulation together with exercise for long-lasting arm pain (B). The review in American Family Physician, however, states that manipulation cannot be recommended. Traction and manipulation are not used when there are signs of spinal cord compression.
tur44-63: Ask your physician which painkillers are suitable for you. In selected patients, injections targeting the nerve root may be given on a physician's decision.
tur44-64: If there is increasing weakness, signs of spinal cord compression, or arm pain that disrupts daily life despite about 6–8 weeks of appropriate treatment, assessment by a neurosurgeon or orthopaedic surgeon is needed.
tur44-65: The neck pain guideline of the Orthopaedic Section of the American Physical Therapy Association (APTA) (JOSPT, 2017) and the review of non-surgical treatment published in American Family Physician (AFP, 2010), side by side. The letters in brackets are the recommendation grades in the JOSPT guideline (B moderate, C weak evidence); treatment is chosen for each person.
tur44-67: Teaching movement and neck stabilisation exercises, laser and a short-term neck collar may be considered (C).
tur44-69: Short-term (one week) immobilisation in a neck collar may ease arm pain; it has not been shown to change the course of the condition.
tur44-71: Intermittent mechanical traction, stretching and strengthening exercises and neck–upper back mobilisation or manipulation together (B).
tur44-72: Traction is most useful once the initial muscle pain has eased; it should not be used if there are signs of spinal cord compression. There is no high-quality evidence for manipulation, and it cannot be recommended because of the risk of rare serious complications.
tur44-74: Education and advice; encouraging participation in work and physical activities (B).
tur44-76: Generally good. In a classic study that followed 51 patients for 2–19 years, 43% had no symptoms after a few months, 29% had mild or intermittent symptoms and 27% had more disabling pain; none developed spinal cord compression. Symptoms may persist in about a third of people treated without surgery.
tur44-78: Arm symptoms that do not respond to 6 weeks of non-surgical treatment, weakness lasting more than 6 weeks, progressive loss of strength or sensation at any point, signs of spinal cord compression, instability or deformity of the spine.
tur44-79: If arm pain, numbness or tingling increases or spreads towards the fingers during an exercise, stop that exercise. Pain moving back from the arm towards the neck, on the other hand, is often interpreted as a good sign. For strengthening and stretching exercises, you can also see the neck pain page.
tur44-80: Raise your arms out to the sides at shoulder height, elbows bent to 90 degrees, palms facing forward. As you tilt your head to the right, straighten your right elbow and lower your forearm out to the side so your right arm is completely straight. Return to the middle. Then, as you tilt your head to the left, do the same with your left arm. The nerve is tensioned at one end while it slackens at the other, so it glides without being stretched. If your arm pain is severe, start with your arms held lower.
tur44-81: 10 slow repetitions to each side. Stop if pain, numbness or tingling increases
tur44-82: In most people, yes. Symptoms are usually most intense in the first weeks, and most people clearly improve within 4–6 months. During this time, exercise and physiotherapy can help reduce pain and make it easier to return to daily life.
tur44-83: If there is increasing weakness in the arm; signs of spinal cord compression such as clumsy hands or difficulty walking; or arm pain that disrupts daily life despite about 6–8 weeks of appropriate treatment, a surgical assessment is needed. In a population study that followed patients with a pinched nerve causing arm pain, about a quarter had surgery during the follow-up period; most people recover without surgery.
tur44-84: Disc bulging is seen on MRI in the large majority of people without pain; on its own this finding does not mean disease, and if you have no symptoms, treatment is usually not needed. In the same study, spinal cord compression was also seen in 5.3% of people without symptoms; if your report mentions spinal cord compression, talk to the physician who requested the MRI about follow-up. You can look after your neck with regular exercise.
tur44-85: Soft tissue work and gentle mobilisation are generally safe. Sources differ on fast, forceful neck manipulation (cracking): the US physiotherapy guideline recommends mobilisation or manipulation together with exercise for long-lasting arm pain, whereas the review in American Family Physician states that there is no high-quality evidence and, pointing to the rare risk of nerve or spinal cord injury, that manipulation cannot be recommended. Manipulation and traction should not be used when there are signs of spinal cord compression.
tur44-86: The following signs may show that the spinal cord or nerves are seriously affected, or point to another problem.
tur44-87: Arm pain together with chest pain, shortness of breath or sweating (it may come from the heart)
tur44-88: A change in bladder or bowel control, or rapidly increasing weakness in the legs
tur44-89: Neck pain that starts after an accident or fall, especially if you are over 65 or have numbness or weakness in the arms or legs (call for help without moving your neck)
tur44-90: Sudden, severe neck pain or headache together with dizziness, double vision, difficulty speaking or swallowing, or numbness in the face
tur44-91: Fever, a stiff neck and a severe headache together
tur44-92: See a physician the same day or as soon as possible:
tur44-93: Neck and arm pain together with a fever, unexplained weight loss or a history of cancer
tur44-94: For assessment within a few weeks:
tur44-95: Arm pain that disrupts daily life despite 6 weeks of appropriate treatment, or weakness lasting more than 6 weeks

tur44-97: Pain around the kneecap that gets worse going down stairs and squatting: what is patellofemoral pain, how is it recognised and how is it treated? A comparison of two guidelines, a short history, six home exercises and warning signs.
tur44-98: Proportion of adolescents with anterior knee pain at any given time (combined result of two studies)
tur44-99: Minimum time after which the assessment should be reviewed if there is not enough improvement despite regular exercise (2024 guide)
tur44-100: In a follow-up study, those among 60 responding patients who found their recovery unsatisfactory after 5–8 years
tur44-101: Combination of exercises recommended by the international consensus statement (2018)
tur44-102: The kneecap glides in a groove on the front of the thigh bone. Pain appears when the load carried by this joint exceeds what the tissues can tolerate. Imaging usually shows no clear damage; the problem is often explained as an imbalance between load and capacity rather than a structural fault.
tur44-103: Increasing activities such as running, jumping or stairs over a short time is a common trigger; weakness in the hip and thigh muscles is also often present.
tur44-104: The diagnosis is made from your history and an examination; imaging is usually not needed.
tur44-106: According to the summary of the US physiotherapy guideline, pain around the kneecap when squatting, climbing stairs or sitting for a long time is the most accurate finding; if squatting is not painful, patellofemoral pain is unlikely. Reduced outward mobility of the kneecap may support the diagnosis, but its absence does not rule it out; the accuracy of the other proposed tests is insufficient.
tur44-107: Usually not needed; imaging often shows no finding that explains the pain. It may be requested to look for other causes in situations such as pain that started after an injury, locking or marked swelling.
tur44-108: Pain confined to the tendon below the kneecap, pain along the joint line with catching, or limping in children suggest other problems. In children and adolescents, knee pain can also be referred from the hip.
tur44-109: What has become clearer in the last decade
tur44-110: Treatment recommendations for anterior knee pain have become clearer over the last decade through consensus statements and guidelines: exercise and education are at the centre of treatment.
tur44-111: In the long-term follow-up of 310 patients from two randomised trials (BJSM), 57% of the 60 people who answered the questionnaires after 5–8 years reported that their recovery was unsatisfactory (ranging from moderate improvement to worse than ever); pain lasting more than 12 months at the start predicted more pain later.
tur44-112: A consensus statement by international researchers (BJSM) recommended exercise therapy, especially combining hip and knee exercises; mobilisations applied to the knee or lower back on their own, and electrotherapy, were not recommended.
tur44-113: In a systematic review (PLoS One), combining two studies gave a point prevalence of 7.2% in adolescents; for yearly prevalence, single studies reported 22.7% in the general population and 28.9% in adolescents. The authors note that, because evidence is scarce, these estimates remain uncertain.
tur44-114: The guideline of the Academy of Orthopaedic Physical Therapy of the American Physical Therapy Association (APTA) (JOSPT) was published: exercises targeting the muscles at the back of the hip and the front of the thigh came to the fore as the core treatment; no added benefit was seen from knee braces and sleeves, dry needling or manual therapy added to exercise.
tur44-115: A best practice guide (BJSM) prepared using 65 high-quality randomised trials (3,796 people), interviews with 12 patients and 19 experts, and three expert focus groups: the core treatment is knee-targeted exercise supported by education, with hip and knee exercise when needed.
tur44-116: Anterior knee pain does not always go away on its own. In the long-term follow-up of 310 patients from two randomised trials, 57% of the 60 people (19%) who answered the questionnaires after 5–8 years reported that their recovery was unsatisfactory (ranging from moderate improvement to worse than ever). Because those who responded were a small, selected group, this figure is not an estimate for everyone. In the study, pain lasting more than 12 months at the start predicted more pain years later. This is why assessment before the pain becomes long-standing is recommended.
tur44-117: Tape, together with exercise, may reduce pain in the short term; knee braces and sleeves have not been shown to help. Neither replaces exercise.
tur44-118: Knowing why the pain develops and how to adjust the load contributes to the success of treatment.
tur44-119: The guideline of the Academy of Orthopaedic Physical Therapy of the American Physical Therapy Association (APTA) (JOSPT, 2019; from the American Family Physician summary) and the best practice guide published in BJSM (2024), side by side. The guide grades the strength of its recommendations as "very high, high, moderate, low, very low"; treatment is chosen for each person.
tur44-120: Exercises targeting the muscles at the back of the hip and the front of the thigh are the core treatment; weight-bearing and non-weight-bearing exercises are similarly effective; high-volume programmes work better.
tur44-122: Knee-targeted exercise supported by education (strength of recommendation: very high); hip and knee exercise when needed (high). For people who find loading with the knee bent hard to tolerate, hip exercises may be emphasised first.
tur44-123: Reduce pain in the short term (6 weeks) in people whose feet roll inwards more; custom insoles are not better than off-the-shelf ones.
tur44-124: Off-the-shelf insoles (strength of recommendation: high); in people whose pain eases during a short trial with the insoles, adjusted for comfort.
tur44-126: Kneecap taping together with exercise reduces pain in the short term; knee braces and sleeves do not improve outcomes.
tur44-127: Tape (strength of recommendation: low): may be considered if the severity or easy flare-up of the pain makes rehabilitation difficult.
tur44-128: Adding it to exercise does not give better results than exercise alone.
tur44-129: Strength of recommendation moderate: may be considered if the severity of the pain, easy flare-ups or fear of movement are getting in the way of rehabilitation.
tur44-131: Retraining the way you walk and run (for example, reducing running distance or increasing step rate) may improve symptoms.
tur44-132: Strength of recommendation low: if symptoms are linked to a particular way of moving, for example increasing step rate in a runner with a long stride.
tur44-134: Dry needling does not improve outcomes; muscle stimulation (NMES) and blood flow restriction give no added benefit to exercise; acupuncture is not better than sham acupuncture.
tur44-135: Dry needling, vibration therapy and hyaluronic acid injections are not recommended outside clinical research.
tur44-136: In Türkiye only authorised physicians may perform dry needling and acupuncture.
tur44-137: Mild, tolerable pain during the exercises is acceptable; if the pain does not increase the next day, carry on, and if it does, reduce the load next time. Make sure your knee stays in line with your toes and does not drift inwards.
tur44-138: Sit upright on a chair. Slowly straighten your knee and tighten the muscle at the front of your thigh, hold for 3 seconds and lower slowly. If it hurts, work within a pain-free range without fully straightening your knee.
tur44-139: In some people it can ease the pain for a short time; however, according to the international consensus statement, the evidence on this is insufficient. It should be used alongside exercise if needed, not instead of it. A best practice guide published in 2024 states that tape may be considered if the severity or easy flare-up of the pain makes rehabilitation difficult; knee-targeted exercise and education are at the centre of treatment, and if there is not enough improvement despite at least 6 weeks of regular exercise, the assessment should be reviewed. According to the summary of the US physiotherapy guideline, knee braces and sleeves have not been shown to help.
tur44-140: It varies from person to person. The best practice guide published in 2024 recommends that, if there is not enough improvement after a realistic period (at least 6 weeks), the assessment, engagement with the exercises, and whether the treatment matches the severity of the pain should be reviewed. There were no high-quality studies that adequately tested the effect beyond 3 months. In the long term, pain can last for years in some people; in a follow-up study, pain lasting more than 12 months at the start predicted more pain years later. This is why assessment before the pain becomes long-standing and regular exercise are recommended.
tur44-141: The following may point to a problem other than anterior knee pain.
tur44-142: Sudden, marked swelling, redness or warmth in the knee, especially together with a fever
tur44-143: Being unable to put weight on the leg after an injury, the knee locking and not straightening, or rapid swelling starting straight away
tur44-144: The kneecap dislocating, or a visible deformity of the knee
tur44-145: Knee or hip pain in children and adolescents together with limping or being unable to walk (the pain may be coming from the hip)
tur44-146: The knee frequently giving way after an injury
tur44-147: Pain that does not ease with rest and wakes you at night, or unexplained weight loss
tur44-148: A hard swelling or lump on the bone
tur44-149: Pain that does not improve despite at least 6 weeks of regular exercise, or that keeps getting worse
